paragraphs.title: The Persecuted Person's Cry to God

easy.explanation: He cries, “My God, my God.”
easy.q: To whom does the speaker cry?

answers: In the daytime and in the night season
easy.explanation: He says, “I cry in the daytime” and “in the night season.”
easy.q: When does the speaker cry to God?

answers: Helping and the words of his roaring
easy.explanation: He asks why God is far from “helping me, and from the words of my roaring.”
easy.q: What does the speaker say is far from him?

medium.explanation: Calling in both the daytime and night season shows continual prayer.
medium.q: What does the repeated crying day and night show?

answers: He continues to cry to God
medium.explanation: Although he feels forsaken, he continues calling upon God.
medium.q: How does the speaker respond to feeling forsaken?

medium.explanation: “Roaring” describes a loud and anguished cry.
medium.q: What does “roaring” most nearly suggest in this passage?

answers: Between crying out and receiving no answer
challenge.explanation: The speaker cries to God but says, “thou hearest not.”
challenge.q: What central tension appears in these verses?

challenge.explanation: The question expresses the speaker’s painful feeling of being abandoned.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “why hast thou forsaken me?” reveal?

answers: It presents God as holy while the speaker describes his distress
It changes from prayer to a military report
It says the speaker no longer believes in God
challenge.explanation: The speaker’s distress is set beside the declaration, “thou art holy.”
challenge.q: How does verse 3 contrast with verses 1–2?

paragraphs.title: The Ancestors' Faith and the Speaker's Humiliation

easy.explanation: The speaker says, “thou art holy.”
easy.q: How is God described in verse 3?

easy.explanation: The text says, “Our fathers trusted in thee.”
easy.q: In whom did the fathers trust?

easy.explanation: They “laugh me to scorn” and despise him.
easy.q: How do those who see the speaker treat him?

answers: God's holiness and the fathers' trust versus the speaker's humiliation
medium.explanation: The fathers trusted and were delivered, while the speaker is mocked and humiliated.
medium.q: What contrast is central to this passage?

answers: To show a history of trusting God
medium.explanation: Their trust and deliverance provide a testimony of God's faithfulness.
medium.q: Why does the speaker recall the fathers?

answers: A feeling of humiliation and worthlessness
A literal description of an animal
medium.explanation: The image presents the speaker as despised and treated as insignificant.
medium.q: What does “a worm, and no man” express?

answers: It shows lifelong dependence upon God
It proves he never needed God
It describes the childhood of his enemies
challenge.explanation: He says God took him from the womb and was his God from his mother's belly.
challenge.q: How does being taken from the womb relate to the speaker's distress?

answers: It intensifies the speaker's isolation and humiliation
It shows that the crowd is celebrating
challenge.explanation: Their scorn, lip-shooting, and head-shaking emphasize his disgrace.
challenge.q: What effect does the enemies' mockery have in the passage?

answers: God's holiness and the fathers' trust, followed by humiliation and dependence from birth
A journey followed by a feast
A battle followed by the division of land
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from God's holiness and past deliverance to the speaker's suffering and lifelong dependence.
challenge.q: What sequence of ideas appears in verses 3–10?

easy.explanation: He says, “Be not far from me.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask God not to do?

easy.explanation: The enemies are portrayed as bulls, a ravening lion, and dogs.
easy.q: Which animals represent the enemies?

answers: They part them and cast lots for his vesture
easy.explanation: They “part my garments” and “cast lots” upon his vesture.
easy.q: What do the enemies do with the speaker's garments?

answers: A sense of enemies surrounding and threatening him
A picture of tame household animals
medium.explanation: The animal images emphasize danger and encirclement.
medium.q: What do the images of bulls, a lion, and dogs create?

answers: Broken down, weakened, and near death
medium.explanation: His bones are out of joint, his heart melts, his strength is dried up, and he is brought into the dust of death.
medium.q: How is the speaker's physical condition described?

medium.explanation: To compass someone is to surround or encircle that person.
medium.q: What does “compassed me” mean?

answers: The external threat deepens the sense of inward collapse
The enemies make the speaker feel victorious
challenge.explanation: The surrounding enemies are described together with the speaker's failing body and strength.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the bodily images and the enemies?

challenge.explanation: Dividing his garments and casting lots for his vesture add public humiliation.
challenge.q: What humiliation is added to the physical danger?

answers: Many forms of danger surrounding the speaker
A change to a festive atmosphere
challenge.explanation: The successive images present varied and multiplying threats.
challenge.q: What does the movement from bulls to a lion to dogs emphasize?

easy.explanation: He says, “O my strength, haste thee to help me.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask God to do?

answers: The sword, the dog, the lion, and the unicorns
easy.explanation: He asks deliverance from the sword, the dog, the lion, and the horns of the unicorns.
easy.q: From what does the speaker ask to be delivered?

easy.explanation: The speaker says, “thou hast heard me.”
easy.q: What does the speaker say God has done at the end of the passage?

medium.explanation: The phrase is an urgent request for God to act quickly.
medium.q: What does “haste thee” reveal about the speaker's condition?

answers: It turns the description of danger into a direct plea for rescue
It changes to a discussion of farming
It cancels the description of the enemies
medium.explanation: After describing the surrounding enemies, the speaker asks God to deliver him.
medium.q: How does this passage connect with the preceding verses?

medium.explanation: “My darling” refers to the speaker's treasured life or soul.
medium.q: What does “my darling” most nearly mean in “Deliver my soul”?

answers: The speaker moves from requesting help to declaring that he has been heard
He moves from salvation to complete despair
He moves from prayer to silence
challenge.explanation: He asks God to save him and then says, “thou hast heard me.”
challenge.q: What change occurs between the plea and the final statement?

answers: To stress the magnitude of the danger
challenge.explanation: The sword, dog, lion, and unicorns represent the dangers from which he seeks rescue.
challenge.q: Why are several enemy images repeated in this plea?

answers: The speaker regards God as the source of his power
The speaker does not know God
The speaker seeks strength from his enemies
challenge.explanation: The title “my strength” expresses dependence upon God.
challenge.q: What does calling God “my strength” imply?

paragraphs.title: Salvation and Praise in the Assembly

answers: Only the names of his enemies
easy.explanation: He says, “I will declare thy name unto my brethren.”
easy.q: What does the speaker promise to declare?

answers: The kings of the nations only
easy.explanation: He addresses “Ye that fear the LORD.”
easy.q: Whom does the speaker call to praise the LORD?

answers: In the midst of the congregation
In the house of his enemies
easy.explanation: He will praise God in the congregation and pay his vows before those who fear Him.
easy.q: Where will the speaker praise God and pay his vows?

answers: The movement from distress to praise and testimony
The movement from praise to silence
The movement from salvation to persecution
medium.explanation: The speaker now declares God's name and calls others to praise Him.
medium.q: What major change appears from the beginning of the psalm to this passage?

answers: To share God's deliverance with others
To mock those who fear God
medium.explanation: His praise becomes a public testimony before the gathered people.
medium.q: Why does the speaker praise God in the congregation?

answers: Promises made to God that the speaker will fulfill
medium.explanation: A vow is a solemn promise or commitment made to God.
medium.q: What are “vows” in this context?

answers: It presents God's response as an accomplished deliverance
It shows that the speaker has stopped praying
It says the enemies have triumphed
challenge.explanation: The statement presents God's hearing and rescue as already experienced.
challenge.q: What does the past-tense statement “thou hast heard me” contribute to the passage?

answers: The speaker declares it and praises God before the congregation
challenge.explanation: He tells his brethren and praises God in the great congregation.
challenge.q: How does personal salvation become a public act?

answers: Both occur in the setting of public praise before God's people
They are unrelated in the passage
challenge.explanation: The speaker pays his vows before those who fear God as part of his worship.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between fearing God and paying vows?

paragraphs.title: Blessing for the Humble and God's Universal Kingship

easy.explanation: The text says, “The meek shall eat and be satisfied.”
easy.q: Who shall eat and be satisfied?

answers: All the ends of the world and the kindreds of the nations
easy.explanation: The passage includes all the ends of the world and all the kindreds of the nations.
easy.q: Who will turn unto the LORD and worship before Him?

easy.explanation: The text says, “the kingdom is the LORD'S.”
easy.q: To whom does the kingdom belong?

answers: Satisfaction is joined with praising the LORD
medium.explanation: The meek eat and are satisfied, and they praise the LORD.
medium.q: What is the relationship between eating and praise?

answers: It moves from blessing a humble group to worship by all nations
It moves from the world to one family only
It moves from praise to mockery
medium.explanation: The passage broadens from the meek to all the ends of the world and nations.
medium.q: How does the vision expand from the meek to the whole world?

answers: Those who enjoy abundance and prosperity
Those who are weak and powerless
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to people who are prosperous or well supplied.
medium.q: What does “fat upon earth” mean in context?

answers: God's rule extends over the nations and the whole earth
God's kingdom is limited to one group
challenge.explanation: The passage says the kingdom is the LORD'S and that He is governor among the nations.
challenge.q: What view of God's kingship is presented?

answers: The worldwide extent of worship and remembrance
challenge.explanation: The phrase points to the farthest parts of the earth and a universal response.
challenge.q: What does “all the ends of the world” emphasize?

answers: Both recognize their dependence upon God and respond in worship
Both are described as God's enemies
challenge.explanation: The passage joins humble satisfaction with universal submission and worship.
challenge.q: How are the meek and those who bow before God connected?

easy.explanation: The text says, “A seed shall serve him.”
easy.q: Who shall serve the LORD?

easy.explanation: They shall declare His righteousness.
easy.q: What shall future generations declare?

answers: A people that shall be born
easy.explanation: The passage speaks of “a people that shall be born.”
easy.q: Who shall hear about what God has done?

answers: The testimony of God's righteousness and deeds
Only the names of the enemies
medium.explanation: Future generations will declare God's righteousness and what He has done.
medium.q: What is passed from one generation to another?

answers: Remembering God's works supports the worship of future generations
Declaring His works ends His worship
medium.explanation: The seed serves God while the message of His righteousness reaches later generations.
medium.q: How are serving God and declaring His works related?

medium.explanation: Here “seed” refers figuratively to descendants and future generations.
medium.q: What does “a seed” mean in this passage?

answers: So that those not yet born may know His works and salvation
To stop people from serving God
challenge.explanation: The passage ensures that a people yet to be born will hear what God has done.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of declaring God's righteousness to future people?

answers: Service to God, declaration of His righteousness, and witness to future generations
Division of garments followed by silence
challenge.explanation: The verses move from serving God to proclaiming His righteousness to a future people.
challenge.q: What sequence of ideas appears in these verses?

answers: Recognition of God continues from the nations into future generations
It returns only to the enemies
It cancels the idea of God's kingship
challenge.explanation: After describing worldwide worship, the psalm extends that testimony into generations yet unborn.
challenge.q: How does this passage complete the psalm's broader vision?
